Distances through water from receivers to every water cell

Source: R/water_distances.R
water_distances.Rd

Measures, for every receiver and water cell, how far sound travels from the receiver to the cell centre without crossing land. Where the straight line stays in water, the distance is that line. Where land lies on it, the distance is the shortest path through water: straight legs that bend only at corners where water turns round land. The corners form a graph, with an edge between any two that see each other across water, and on that graph the algorithm of Dijkstra (1959) builds the minimal paths from the receiver in order of increasing length. The path starts at the receiver itself, so distance_m is never less than straight_m. In the Stoney example the cell 640 m north-west of station S023 lies across a point of land; its path is 1,955 m.

Usage

water_distances(grid, receivers, max_distance = Inf, control = list())

Arguments

grid

A terra::SpatRaster in a projected CRS with metre units, such as the UTM zone of the lake, or a file path that terra::rast() reads. Only the first layer is used.

receivers

A data frame with a station_id or receiver_serial column and either x and y in the CRS of grid or deploy_lat and deploy_lon in WGS 84; or an sf point object. When x and y carry an epsg attribute it must match the grid. Other columns pass through to the receivers attribute; with both receiver_serial and station_id the rows also form the lookup attribute.

max_distance

The largest distance through water kept, in metres, the unit of the grid's projected CRS. A pair farther apart through water is left out. The default, Inf, keeps every pair connected by water.

control

A list of rarely changed settings:

  • cores: number of processes for parallel::mclapply(), one receiver each. The default is 1. Windows has no forked processes, so there 1 is used, with a warning when more are asked for.

  • path: "exact", the default, for the shortest path through water; "grid" to keep the straight line on clear pairs and take the 8-neighbour grid path where land lies on the line (see NEWS).

  • maxiter: passed to terra::gridDist() when path = "grid". The default is 1000.

Value

A data frame of class water_distances, one row per receiver and water cell within max_distance:

  • cell: the terra cell number of the water cell.

  • station_id or receiver_serial: the receiver key.

  • distance_m: the distance in metres used for detection; never less than straight_m. These are metres on the ground. A grid is refused when its CRS scale at the raster centre is more than 1 percent from 1 on either axis or either diagonal, or cannot be measured, as in a local engineering CRS.

  • straight_m: the straight-line distance in metres.

  • in_water: TRUE where the straight line stays in water, so distance_m equals straight_m; FALSE where land lies on it.

Attributes: grid (the grid, packed by terra::wrap()), cells (all water cells), key, receivers (one row per key with the position used, snap_m, n_rows and spread_m), lookup, max_distance and unreachable (pairs that no water path connects, including water joined to the receiver's only through a point where two land cells meet).

Details

The detection curve is read at this distance whether or not land lies on the line; de_model() has a blocked argument for such pairs.

The land rule. One rule tests every straight leg. A leg is blocked when it comes more than a thousandth of a cell side (10 cm on 100 m cells) into land. A point where two land cells meet diagonally counts as land, so a leg through it is blocked. A leg that grazes land by less is clear. The margin gives a receiver a few millimetres off its cell centre the same lines of sight as one at the centre.

Sight one way. A receiver within that margin of such a point can see cells on both sides of it that cannot see it back. No distance changes.

The unreachable cell. Two water cells that touch only where two land cells meet are not joined. In the Stoney example one water cell joins the lake only that way. It gets no row and is counted in the unreachable attribute.

Memory. Lines of sight from the corners are tested in fixed batches of about 200,000 lines. The tests run in passes. With one core, each receiver in turn makes one pass over the corners it reaches that no earlier receiver reached. With several cores, each core makes one pass over its share of the corners within max_distance of any receiver. On the Stoney example with no max_distance and one core, where all lines are tested in one pass, batches of 200,000 lines give a lower peak memory than batches ten times larger, at about the same time. A pass of 200,000 lines or fewer makes the same batches at either size. The script that measures both sizes on that example, each run in its own R process, is https://github.com/jakebrownscombe/detfield/blob/main/validation/04_memory_time.R. Its log is https://github.com/jakebrownscombe/detfield/blob/main/validation/outputs/04_memory_time.log. Both are in the repository and not in the installed package.

Snapping. Cells with a value are water and NA cells are land. Rows of receivers that share a key are averaged to one position. A receiver on a land cell moves to the centre of the nearest water cell when it lies within one cell diagonal of the edge of some water cell; one farther from water is an error. The move is at least half a cell side and at most one and a half cell diagonals: 50 to 212 m on 100 m cells. The warning gives each move in metres, and the receivers attribute keeps it as snap_m.

References

Dijkstra, E. W. (1959). A note on two problems in connexion with graphs. Numerische Mathematik, 1, 269-271. doi:10.1007/BF01386390

See also

de_field(), which turns the distances into detection probabilities.

Examples

# The Stoney example: Stoney Lake (100 m cells, land NA) and 70 receivers.
tif <- system.file("extdata", "stoney_depth.tif", package = "detfield")
grid <- terra::rast(tif)
# Pairs beyond 2 km are left out, which keeps the example fast.
d <- water_distances(grid, stoney_track$receivers, max_distance = 2000)
d
#> <water_distances> 49,214 pairs: 70 receivers (by station_id) x 4,818
#>   water cells
#> Straight line used for 39,931 of 49,214 pairs; longest distance 2,000 m
#>    cell station_id distance_m straight_m in_water
#> 1 17483       S001   1968.380   1923.538    FALSE
#> 2 17651       S001   1871.543   1835.756    FALSE
#> 3 17652       S001   1911.151   1886.796    FALSE
#> 4 17653       S001   1957.381   1941.649    FALSE
#> 5 17819       S001   1778.762   1749.286    FALSE
#> 6 17820       S001   1821.723   1802.776    FALSE
# The cell 640 m north-west of S023 lies across a point of land; the path
# goes round it, 1,955 m against 640 m in a straight line.
north_west <- terra::cellFromXY(grid, cbind(724054, 4936291))
d[d$station_id == "S023" & d$cell == north_west, ]
#> <water_distances> 1 pair: 70 receivers (by station_id) x 4,818 water
#>   cells
#> Straight line used for 0 of 1 pairs; longest distance 1,955 m
#>   cell station_id distance_m straight_m in_water
#> 1 9446       S023   1954.619   640.3124    FALSE
